title: What an alarm tells us—and what it does not
account:
During a fictional equipment discussion, a learner describes an infusion pump displaying a downstream-occlusion message during a training exercise. The learner says a section of the demonstration tubing was caught under a training pad. A colleague points out that the recorded message and the observed tubing position should both be retained; neither alone proves a complete explanation for the alarm.

The device manufacturer, model, settings, and exact alarm wording are not available. The conversation does not contain a verified device-specific troubleshooting procedure. For that reason this entry records the observation and the missing context without turning it into instructions to bypass a safety mechanism or resume a patient's infusion.

The useful practical lesson is to retain the circumstances around an interruption. The learner proposes checking the approved manual with a supervisor before developing a local checklist. That proposal is recorded as a future action. The recording does not establish that the manual was checked or the alarm was resolved.

facts.text: In the synthetic training exercise, tubing was described as caught under a pad while an occlusion message was displayed.
Reviewing the correct device manual with a supervisor was proposed; this was not patient treatment.
Device model, approved response, and final resolution were not captured.

questions: What manufacturer and model was in use?
What does its approved manual say?
conclusions: Preserve the event as an observation, not a validated troubleshooting procedure.
